h1: Why beer tastes flat from a plastic cup at events
title: Why beer tastes flat in plastic cups | Craft Beer School
desc: Beer from a plastic cup at events often tastes flat and dull. The cup, the pour, the heat and the kegs all play a part. Here is what is going on.
teaser: That festival beer tasted great at the brewery. In a plastic cup in the sun it tastes flat. The cup is only part of the story.
standfirst: Plastic cups are cheap, light and safe in a crowd. They are also hard on beer. Here is why event beer so often tastes flat and dull, plus what you can do about it.
sections: Event beer has a lot going against it

A beer at a festival or concert has had a hard day before it reaches you. The kegs may have been driven across a hot city, set up in a tent and run through a portable chiller pushed far beyond its normal load. The bartender is pouring fast for a long queue. Then the beer goes into a thin plastic cup and you carry it into the sun.

Each step takes something away. The cup gets the blame because it is the obvious difference, but the cup, the pour, the dispense system and the heat all work together.

Plastic surfaces are rarely as smooth or as clean as a beer clean glass. Cups often carry traces of the oils or release agents used in moulding, plus dust from storage. Those residues break down foam, so the head collapses quickly. Scratches and rough spots also give carbon dioxide places to form bubbles, so gas leaves the beer faster.

Thin cups are also flexible. Squeezing the cup as you hold it can push up more foam and gas. And most plastic cups are straight sided, with no shape to gather aroma toward your nose. Less aroma makes beer taste duller, because much of what we call flavour is smell.

At a busy bar, beer is often poured fast and from a height into a dry cup. That foams it hard, knocking gas out of the beer and into a head that collapses in a minute. To save time, some bartenders then pour off the foam and top up with more beer, which loses still more carbonation.

Temporary dispense systems also struggle. Kegs that are too warm or gas pressure set wrong lead to foamy pours from the tap, so the bartender pours slowly or wastes beer. Our guide on why the same beer tastes different on draught and in a can explains how much dispense matters.

Outdoor events in India often mean 30 °C or more. A thin plastic cup does little to protect beer from that. A 4 °C beer held in a warm hand in the sun can be several degrees warmer within ten minutes. Warm beer holds less carbon dioxide, so it goes flat faster. It also tastes sweeter and heavier.

A large 500 ml cup makes this worse. The last third of a big cup is often warm and flat by the time you reach it. Our guide on why a beer tastes sweeter as it warms explains what heat does to flavour.
It is not always the cup

Sometimes the beer was flat before it reached the cup. A keg that has been shaken in transport and tapped straight away pours foamy and loses gas. A keg left in the sun before the event may be warm when tapped. No chiller fully fixes that in a busy tent. Beer from a keg that has been open on a quiet bar for two days can also taste tired.

One way to tell: look at the beer when it is first poured. If it has fine bubbles rising and a decent head that fades fast, the cup and the heat are the main problem. If it pours with almost no bubbles at all, the problem started in the keg or the lines. Spotting where a fault comes from is a big part of tasting like a professional. It is also a skill you can train.
What you can do as a drinker

• Choose a smaller cup and come back for another. A small pour stays cold and fizzy to the end.
  • Hold the cup by the rim or the base, not with your whole hand around it.
  • Find shade before you drink, not after.
  • Ask for a pour down the side of the cup if the bar is not too busy.
  • If the event offers a reusable cup or a proper glass, take it.

Drink water between beers too. Heat and crowds dehydrate you fast. A dry palate tastes less.

Organisers have more control. Reusable hard plastic cups, washed and rinsed well, are better than thin disposables and create less waste. Kegs should be cold before the event starts, ideally at the serving temperature. A shaded bar, a cold water rinse for cups and smaller pour sizes all help.

For craft beer festivals, many organisers use small tasting glasses of 100 to 200 ml. They let people try more styles without drinking more. The beer stays cold and fresh in each small pour.
Taste it at home to see the difference

Pour one can of a beer you know into a clean glass and another into a thin plastic cup. Taste both at the same temperature. Then leave the plastic cup in your hand for ten minutes and taste again. You will see exactly how much the cup and the heat cost the beer.
faqs: Why does beer go flat in plastic cups?
Plastic cups often carry residues that break down foam. Their surfaces release carbon dioxide faster. Fast pours and heat at events make it worse.
Does beer taste different in plastic?
Often, yes. Straight sided plastic cups gather less aroma and the beer tends to warm and go flat faster, which dulls the flavour.
How can I make event beer taste better?
Ask for a smaller pour, find shade, hold the cup by the rim and drink it while it is still cold.
